content.text:
Use UTC half-open intervals as the durable definition of what a digest contains, and treat scheduler invocations as merely opportunities to process an occurrence—not as the occurrence itself.

## Documented facts

- Laravel supports per-task time zones, but explicitly warns that, in time zones with DST, a scheduled task “may run twice or even not run at all,” and recommends avoiding timezone scheduling where possible.
- PostgreSQL ranges have explicit inclusive/exclusive bounds; [ means inclusive and ) exclusive. PostgreSQL’s own range partitioning also uses inclusive-lower/exclusive-upper semantics so adjacent partitions share a boundary without overlap.
- AWS describes transactional outbox as solving the database-write-plus-message “dual write” problem. It also states that duplicate events may be sent and consumers should be idempotent by tracking processed messages.

## Application design: time windows

Persist each digest occurrence with an immutable key, for example:
```
digest:tenant-42:user-7:daily:2026-09-15T09:00:00Z
```
and a UTC tstzrange such as:
```
[2026-09-14 09:00:00+00, 2026-09-15 09:00:00+00)
```
Query with:
```
WHERE occurred_at >= :start_utc AND occurred_at < :end_utc
```
The half-open rule gives every event exactly one bucket: an event precisely at end belongs to the next digest, never both. UTC intervals are monotonic and unambiguous, unlike local “02:30” during DST.
If the product promise is “9:00 local time,” retain the IANA zone and local recurrence rule, define/document a DST policy, then materialize each intended occurrence to a UTC start/end pair and stable key. A fall-back hour can map one wall-clock time to two instants; a spring-forward wall-clock time may not exist. The key must represent your chosen logical occurrence—for example, local date plus rule and a documented “earlier offset” / “shift forward” policy—not a transient cron wake-up.

## Catch-up after wake-up completion

Do not mark a wake-up key as terminal proof that all eligible rows have arrived. A late transaction can commit after the worker read the window, or be backfilled with an occurred_at inside an already completed interval.
A robust SQL design separates:
- digest_occurrences: (occurrence_key UNIQUE, start_at, end_at, status)
- source events with immutable event IDs and occurred_at
- digest_items: UNIQUE(occurrence_key, source_event_id)
- outbox: durable pending delivery intent
On every periodic wake-up, rescan a bounded look-back horizon of completed/recent occurrences and insert missing items idempotently:
```
INSERT INTO digest_items (occurrence_key, source_event_id) SELECT o.key, e.id FROM digest_occurrences o JOIN events e ON e.occurred_at >= o.start_at AND e.occurred_at < o.end_at WHERE o.end_at > now() - interval '7 days' ON CONFLICT (occurrence_key, source_event_id) DO NOTHING;
```
Then either revise an unsent digest or emit a documented late-item follow-up. This is application policy; the database constraint makes the repair repeat-safe.

## Delivery remains at-least-once

A transactional outbox atomically records “this occurrence needs sending” with its database state, avoiding loss from a crash between commit and enqueue. But it cannot atomically commit with an external email/push provider. A timeout after the provider accepted the request is an unknown outcome: retrying may duplicate; not retrying may lose delivery.
Therefore use the occurrence key as the provider idempotency key when supported, persist attempt/request IDs and states (pending, accepted, unknown, failed), reconcile unknown outcomes when the provider exposes status lookup, and make retries safe. AWS’s duplicate-message guidance applies directly here: outbox publication and downstream processing remain at-least-once, so deduplication is required.

Sources:
1. [laravel](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/scheduling)
2. [aws.amazon](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)
